DQN

A deep Q-network is Q-learning (Lesson 52) with a neural network in place of the table. The screen goes in, one value per action comes out, and the agent picks the largest. Mnih et al. (2015) trained one network design, with the same settings, on 49 Atari games.

Catch

A ball falls one row per step. Move the paddle (green) under it: $+1$ for a catch, $-1$ for a miss. The network sees the 49 pixels and outputs $Q(s, a)$ for left, stay and right. Click a pixel to move the ball, or the bottom row to move the paddle, and watch the values change.

49 pixels → 32 hidden units → 3 values

The Atari network

The architecture from Mnih et al. (2015). The input is the last 4 frames, each converted to greyscale and shrunk to $84 \times 84$. One frame cannot show which way a ball is moving, so a stack of four is used to make the state closer to Markov (Lesson 15). Click a layer.

The maths

The network $Q(s, a; \boldsymbol\theta)$ takes a state and outputs one number for each action. One forward pass gives all of $Q(s, \cdot\,; \boldsymbol\theta)$, so the greedy action and the $\max$ in the Q-learning target cost a single evaluation.

DQN minimises the squared TD error over transitions $(s, a, r, s')$ drawn uniformly from a replay memory $\mathcal{D}$ (Lesson 67):

$$L(\boldsymbol\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{(s,a,r,s') \sim U(\mathcal{D})}\Big[\big(\underbrace{r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a'; \boldsymbol\theta^-)}_{y} - Q(s, a; \boldsymbol\theta)\big)^2\Big].$$

The target $y$ uses older weights $\boldsymbol\theta^-$, copied from $\boldsymbol\theta$ every $C$ updates (Lesson 68). At the end of an episode, $y = r$.

The target is treated as a constant, as in every semi-gradient method (Lesson 62), so the gradient is

$$\nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta} L = -2\,\mathbb{E}\big[(y - Q(s, a; \boldsymbol\theta))\, \nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta} Q(s, a; \boldsymbol\theta)\big].$$

Only the output for the action actually taken gets an error signal. The other outputs change only through the weights they share.

The agent acts ε-greedily. In the paper, ε falls from 1 to 0.1 over the first million frames. Other settings: discount 0.99, minibatch 32, replay memory of the last 1,000,000 transitions, $C = 10{,}000$, each action repeated for 4 frames, and rewards clipped to $[-1, 1]$ so one step size works across games.

DQN has all three legs of Lesson 65's deadly triad: a neural network, bootstrapped targets, and off-policy learning from old data. Replay and the target network are what kept it stable enough to work.

A convolutional layer with $k \times k$ filters, stride $t$ and $C_{\text{out}}$ filters, applied to an $n \times n \times C_{\text{in}}$ input (no padding), gives

$$n_{\text{out}} = \frac{n - k}{t} + 1, \qquad \text{parameters} = k \cdot k \cdot C_{\text{in}} \cdot C_{\text{out}} + C_{\text{out}}.$$

Each filter has a weight for every position and input channel it covers, plus a bias. The same filter slides across the whole image, which is why the convolutional layers are small and the first fully connected layer holds most of the parameters.

The Catch agent is a scaled-down DQN: a fully connected network instead of a convolutional one, Adam instead of RMSProp, replay memory 5,000, minibatch 32, $C = 100$, $\gamma = 0.99$, and ε falling from 1 to 0.1 over 500 episodes.
